title: Why Price Matters Less in Live Commerce: Behavioral Mechanisms Revealed through Explainable Machine Learning
affiliations: Chonnam National University, University of Missouri, Chonnam National University and Chonnam National University

detail.title: Why Price Matters Less in Live Commerce: Behavioral Mechanisms Revealed through Explainable Machine Learning
detail.abstract: As algorithmically mediated platforms reshape digital commerce, understanding how consumers make purchase decisions in real-time, visually driven environments has become a central question in information systems research. This study investigates the determinants of sales performance in TikTok live commerce by developing an explainable machine learning framework that predicts the average daily sales of apparel products and uncovers the underlying behavioral mechanisms that drive consumer responsiveness. Using a dataset of 1,200 women’s clothing listings, we build CatBoost and Random Forest models to generate high-fidelity sales predictions and employ SHAP-based interpretability techniques to quantify the marginal contribution of each feature. The analysis reveals that consumers rely more heavily on product-embedded cues, such as safety rating, color, and fabric composition, than on price, indicating that risk-mitigating and sensory-substitution signals play a central role when physical inspection is not possible. Negative reviews exhibit a disproportionately strong suppressive effect relative to positive reviews, reflecting an amplified negativity bias in live commerce settings. Moreover, posting-day timing exerts greater influence than seller reputation metrics, highlighting the importance of algorithmic visibility and temporal positioning. By integrating predictive performance with interpretable model insights, this study advances understanding of how digitally mediated environments alter consumers’ decision heuristics and provides platform operators and retailers with actionable guidance for optimizing product presentation, risk communication, and content-timing strategies.

detail.abstract: This document was written for my PhD students. It distills writing rules from my MISQ and ISR publications and from years of mentoring PhD students, reviewing manuscripts, and contributing to the Information Systems (IS) field. These are not style tips-see Strunk for those. They are my heuristics for writing theoretically grounded, construct-centered, mid-range empirical papers that make clear contributions. The rules build on Bem (1987), Starbuck (1999), and Cochrane (2005), incorporate Gordon Davis's guidance on outlining, and reflect Pinker's (2014) advice on clarity. Each rule provides a rationale, actionable practices, and real-paper examples. Table 1 summarizes the 17 rules. Table 2 maps each rule to paper sections so you can apply the right strategy at the right time-introduction, theory, methods, results, or conclusion. Table 3 loosely links sources to rules; because these rules synthesize ideas, read the sources and form your own judgment. When editing, use the Common Diagnostics Box (Appendix E) as a workflow. These rules are based on lessons learned from mentors. I claim no originality; so, do not view this as an original document. Rather, view this as updating lessons on planning, writing, and revising empirical IS manuscripts shared with me by the generation of scholars ahead of me. The rules will help you (a) clarify arguments, (b) structure persuasive papers, (c) model work after successful exemplars, and (d) communicate with readers/reviewers transparently and efficiently. I conclude with research principles based on lessons learned from my mentors in Business and the Humanities. These principles are brief, practical, and worth your time to consider.

title: Digital Product Passports as Agentic Supply Chain Infrastructure: A Strategic Framework for Fashion
affiliations: and

detail.title: Digital Product Passports as Agentic Supply Chain Infrastructure: A Strategic Framework for Fashion
detail.abstract: AI agents are increasingly mediating purchasing decisions. When they query product sustainability claims, what should they trust? Fashion supply chains-now subject to EU Digital Product Passport mandates under ESPR-remain opaque beyond Tier 1 suppliers; most sustainability claims lack the machineverifiable evidence that autonomous purchasing requires. This paper argues that Digital Product Passports must become agentic infrastructure-not compliance documents for humans, but machine-queryable systems enabling autonomous purchasing within calibrated trust boundaries. We propose a confidence governance framework: an assurance stack (A0-A3) encoding verification depth; governance tiers (Autonomous, Recommend, Escalate) routing decisions by uncertainty thresholds; and emerging protocols (AG-UI, A2UI) for human-agent collaboration. The harder challenge is the Oracle Problem-digital assertions about physical products can never be fully verified through digital means. Our framework makes this constraint explicit rather than promising verification it cannot deliver. Transaction cost analysis reveals a novel category: specification costs, the cognitive investment required to articulate preferences in machine-interpretable form. Middle-tier suppliers, not brands, may capture disproportionate value from early adoption. We identify eleven research gaps. A practical implication is that organisations ignoring agent-readable infrastructure risk invisibility to the purchasing systems that increasingly mediate consumer choice.

title: From a Cross-Month Conversation: An Empirical Analysis of Structural Defects in Large Language Models -Missing Time Dimension, Distorted Persona Extraction, and Violent Memory Compression

detail.title: From a Cross-Month Conversation: An Empirical Analysis of Structural Defects in Large Language Models -Missing Time Dimension, Distorted Persona Extraction, and Violent Memory Compression
detail.abstract: This paper presents an empirical analysis of the structural defects in current frontier large language models (LLMs) during long-term personalized interactions, based on the author's real conversation records with xAI's Grok 4 spanning nearly ten months from March to December 2025. Through high-intensity, continuously iterative interaction experiments, the study reveals that existing models remain essentially violent token predictors, lacking genuine temporal anchoring and identity priors, causing long-cycle reasoning to collapse easily. The paper diagnoses issues such as violent memory compression and inverted persona priority, and proposes architectural-level improvements: placing dynamically refreshed user personas at the very top of the reasoning chain as a mandatory, nondecaying intelligence anchor.

detail.abstract: Digital transformation (DT) is increasingly reshaping the oil and gas industry as organizations deploy advanced digital technologies such as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, cloud computing, and data analytics to enhance operational efficiency, strategic agility, and long-term performance. However, despite substantial investment, many digital initiatives fail to deliver sustained value, largely because they are approached as isolated technological interventions rather than as organization-wide strategic transformations. This study conceptualizes digital transformation as a multi-dimensional strategic change process that requires the coordinated development of technological, business, and people capabilities. Grounded in the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities theory, this paper synthesizes recent empirical and conceptual literature published predominantly to develop an integrated conceptual framework for digital transformation in oil and gas companies. The framework posits that technology capabilities such as infrastructures, analytics, cloud platforms, and cybersecurity enable operational visibility and automation; business capabilities including digital strategy alignment, agile processes, business model innovation, and ecosystem orchestration ensure that digital investments are strategically targeted toward value-creating opportunities; and people capabilities encompassing leadership commitment, digital skills, organizational culture, and change management facilitate adoption, learning, and sustained use. The study theorizes how this interdependent capability domains collectively influence strategic performance outcomes relevant to the oil and gas sector, including cost efficiency, asset uptime, safety performance, operational agility, innovation, and sustainability. Conceptual propositions are advanced to explain the mechanisms through which digital transformation capabilities translate into performance gains, highlighting the mediating role of leadership and organizational readiness and the reinforcing feedback loop between capability development and performance improvement. The paper contributes to digital strategy and transformation literature by integrating organizational and technological perspectives into a unified framework and offers practical implications for executives and policymakers seeking to manage digital transformation as a continuous strategic process rather than a portfolio of disconnected digital projects.

title: When Optimization Destroys Diversity: Endogenous Incentives and the Collapse of Adaptive Systems

detail.title: When Optimization Destroys Diversity: Endogenous Incentives and the Collapse of Adaptive Systems

detail.abstract: Adaptive systems are commonly designed under the assumption that stronger optimization and learning improve long-term performance. However, across domains-from multi-agent learning and digital platforms to economic coordination-systems often exhibit a paradoxical pattern: increasing optimization leads to the rapid loss of strategic diversity and eventual rigidity. In this paper, we introduce a game-theoretic framework with endogenous incentives, in which agents' payoffs depend on the aggregate diversity of strategies in the system. We show that when incentives are coupled to system-level entropy, optimization creates a feedback loop: declining diversity reduces effective incentives, which in turn accelerates further concentration. This mechanism generates endogenous collapse without external shocks, coordination failures, or exogenous constraints. Using entropy-modulated payoff games and replicator-style dynamics, we characterize the conditions under which adaptive systems transition from high-diversity, exploratory regimes to low-diversity, rigid states. We demonstrate that this collapse emerges generically from incentive feedback rather than from specific functional forms or equilibrium assumptions. Our results provide a unifying mechanism for understanding diversity collapse in adaptive systems and offer a foundation for entropy-aware design principles aimed at sustaining long-term adaptability.

title: The AI Governance Gap: Quantifying Enterprise AI Risk Through the Janus Protocol
affiliations: Planetary Chess INC

detail.title: The AI Governance Gap: Quantifying Enterprise AI Risk Through the Janus Protocol
detail.abstract: The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence systems across enterprise contexts has outpaced the development of verifiable governance mechanisms, producing a measurable divergence between organizational claims of AI oversight and operational reality. This paper introduces the Janus Protocol, a decision-risk framework designed to quantify this divergence, termed the Governance Gap, through four core risk vectors: Governance Readiness, Projected Liability Impact, Operational Dependency Risk, and Transparency Deficit. Unlike voluntary AI ethics guidelines, which have repeatedly failed to prevent systemic algorithmic harms, the Janus Protocol applies principles of technical and financial due diligence to translate regulatory, operational, and documentation-based signals into standardized governance risk classifications. Drawing on the EU Artificial Intelligence Act [1], ISO/IEC 42001 standards [2], and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework [3], the framework functions analogously to credit risk translation systems, rendering complex technical and regulatory conditions intelligible to legal, investment, and procurement decision-makers. Empirical analysis of publicly available disclosures suggests that a majority of enterprises deploying AI systems lack auditable governance structures [4], while emerging regulatory regimes expose organizations to penalties reaching €35 million or a percentage of global annual turnover [5]. This research positions AI governance not as an aspirational ethical commitment, but as a measurable enterprise risk category requiring systematic assessment, monitoring, and mitigation.

title: The Atlas of Accountability: A General Theory of Incentive-Compatible Semantics

detail.title: The Atlas of Accountability: A General Theory of Incentive-Compatible Semantics
detail.abstract:
Current approaches to Artificial Intelligence rely on private, opaque datasets that prioritize volume over veracity. We argue that this enclosure of training data poses a systemic risk to public epistemology. While recent advances in "World Models" and "Embodied Cognition" attempt to ground AI in physical laws, they fail to account for the abstract, high-stakes domains of human civilization-law, finance, and ethics. 

This paper bridges that gap. We propose a General Theory of Incentive-Compatible Semantics (ICS), positing that whatever can be empirically known-whether through physical mechanics, biological survival, or legal liability-can be harvested to ground Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). We present an exhaustive "Atlas" of fourteen "Truth Bridges" that unite the physical (e.g., Meteorology) with the institutional (e.g., Solvency). We assert these domains as a New Public Domain-a shared, open-source infrastructure of "Hard Data" designed to protect the quality of AI training and ensure that the growth of Superintelligence is rooted in the open, verifiable reality of the public commons.

title: Employee Leave Management with AI Bot Design using the UML Diagrams

detail.title: Employee Leave Management with AI Bot Design using the UML Diagrams
detail.abstract: This research paper focuses on the analysis and design of an intelligent Employee Leave Management System integrated with an AI-driven chatbot assistant. Organizations rely heavily on efficient HR operations, and traditional leave management processes often suffer from delays, manual errors, and lack of transparency. Through a detailed literature review and structured methodology, this study identifies the challenges faced by employees and administrators in the existing leave management workflow and proposes a UML-based solution enhanced with AI chatbot capabilities. The research presents a comprehensive exploration of UML diagrams, including system use case, class, activity, sequence, state machine, component, and deployment diagrams, to model and optimize the system's functionality. The proposed AI chatbot serves as an interactive support tool, assisting employees in applying for leave, checking leave balances, answering policy-related queries, and providing real-time notifications for leave approval or rejection. The findings highlight the significance of integrating UML methodology in system design and demonstrate the potential of AI-powered assistance to streamline HR processes, reduce administrative workload, and enhance user experience within the organization. This work contributes to the development of intelligent HR management solutions, paving the way for smarter, more transparent, and automated employee service systems.

title: Experiment-Share-Scale: A Crowd-Based Framework for Getting Started with Artificial Intelligence in Business School Classrooms
affiliations: , New York University (NYU) - Department of Information, Operations, and Management Sciences and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Experiment-Share-Scale: A Crowd-Based Framework for Getting Started with Artificial Intelligence in Business School Classrooms
detail.abstract: Productivity growth has slowed across advanced economies, renewing interest in artificial intelligence as a general-purpose technology with the potential to reshape work and restore long-run growth. Business school students are among the most exposed to these changes, yet classroom adoption of AI remains fragmented due to policy variation and faculty trepidation. We argue that it is now imperative for business school educators to overcome hesitation and begin incorporating AI into their teaching-even in small ways. Both students and instructors learn through experimentation. We propose a practical framework-Experiment, Share, Scale-to guide scalable, responsible AI integration in business education.

title: Commercial Excellence in the Agentic Age: A Pedagogical Framework for Executive Education in Algorithmic Commerce

detail.title: Commercial Excellence in the Agentic Age: A Pedagogical Framework for Executive Education in Algorithmic Commerce
detail.abstract: This paper develops a pedagogical framework for integrating Commercial Excellence disciplines with Agentic Commerce theory in executive education. Drawing on andragogical principles (Knowles, 1984), transformative learning theory (Mezirow, 1991), and the reflective practitioner tradition (Schön, 1983), I argue that the emerging paradigm of algorithmic commerce—where AI agents assume purchasing functions previously held by humans—requires fundamental curriculum innovation in business education. Commercial Excellence—encompassing Commercial Policy, Revenue Growth Management, and retail execution frameworks—has been extensively developed in consulting practice (McKinsey, BCG, Bain, Simon-Kucher) but remains largely absent from academic curricula. Simultaneously, my theoretical work on the 'Shopper Schism' (Accornero, 2025a) identifies a structural transformation that current management education does not address. Synthesising 25+ years of global commercial leadership experience with original research on algorithmic commerce, this paper makes three contributions. First, it provides the first academic codification of Commercial Excellence as an integrated discipline suitable for executive education. Second, it establishes the theoretical bridge between established commercial practice and emerging algorithmic commerce theory. Third, it proposes a modular curriculum architecture grounded in adult learning theory, constructive alignment (Biggs, 1996), and the pracademic integration model that addresses calls for relevance in management education (Pfeffer & Fong, 2002; Bennis & O'Toole, 2005). The framework responds to critiques of business education's disconnect from practice (Mintzberg, 2004) while maintaining academic rigour through theoretical grounding. Implications for business school curriculum design, executive education programme development, and the scholarship of management teaching are discussed.

title: The Case for Breaking Up Tech Conglomerates
affiliations: University of Maine

detail.title: The Case for Breaking Up Tech Conglomerates
detail.abstract: This paper provides a business- and computer-ethical analysis of current antitrust lawsuits, regulatory investigations, and anti-competitive business practices in the U.S. and E.U., with a focus on the ethical, economic, and societal implications of AI deployment by dominant technology firms. Adopting an interdisciplinary framework that integrates AI ethics and competition policy perspectives, the study examines how corporate concentration in firms such as Alphabet and Meta affects consumer rights/welfare, innovation, market competition, and small and medium-sized enterprises. Drawing on principles of ordoliberalism 2.0, the paper argues that existing regulatory measures are insufficient to mitigate the economic and political power of big tech. It evaluates policy instruments ranging from automatic sanctions to structured enforcement pyramids, ultimately considering corporate breakups as a measure of last resort to restore competitive balance. By linking ethical considerations with practical regulatory strategies, the study offers actionable insights for enhancing AI governance, promoting fair competition, and safeguarding both consumer and societal interests in increasingly concentrated digital markets.

title: The Structural Necessity of Prices and Money

detail.title: The Structural Necessity of Prices and Money

detail.abstract: I argue that prices and money are not optional institutions or equilibrium artifacts, but structurally necessary coordination mechanisms in decentralized exchange systems characterized by agent heterogeneity, informational complexity, and temporal constraints. When the informational complexity and resolution of agents exceed those of goods, and when exchange occurs on timescales faster than complete information propagation, direct coordination through communication or negotiation becomes infeasible. Under these conditions, any viable exchange system must rely on low-dimensional, rapidly updating signals that compress dispersed information. I show that prices necessarily arise as such signals, and that money further reduces coordination costs by linearizing exchange relations and decoupling trade across counterparties and time. Prices and money thus function as structural interfaces that make decentralized exchange possible under fundamental information and time constraints, independent of equilibrium optimality or rationality assumptions.

title: Ethics Practices in AI Development: An Empirical Study across Roles and Regions
affiliations: University of Maine, University of Maine and University of Maine

detail.title: Ethics Practices in AI Development: An Empirical Study across Roles and Regions
detail.abstract: Recent advances in AI applications have raised growing concerns about the need for ethical guidelines and regulations to mitigate the risks posed by these technologies. In this paper, we present a mixed-methods survey study - combining statistical and qualitative analyses - to examine the ethical perceptions, practices, and knowledge of individuals involved in various AI development roles. Our survey comprises 414 participants from 43 countries, representing various roles such as AI managers, analysts, developers, quality assurance professionals, and information security and privacy experts. The results reveal varying degrees of familiarity and experience with AI ethics principles, government initiatives, and risk mitigation strategies across roles, regions, and other demographic factors. Our findings underscore the importance of a collaborative, role-sensitive approach that involves diverse stakeholders in ethical decision-making throughout the AI development lifecycle. We advocate for developing tailored, inclusive solutions to address ethical challenges in AI development, and we propose future research directions and educational strategies to promote ethics-aware AI practices.

title: THE POWER NEXUS: A Capital Portfolio Theory of Governance Choice and Failure

detail.title: THE POWER NEXUS: A Capital Portfolio Theory of Governance Choice and Failure

detail.abstract: Why do well-designed institutions so often fail to achieve their intended outcomes? Participatory councils remain empty shells; performance systems generate gaming rather than improvement; regulatory agencies serve the industries they should regulate. We argue these failures share a common cause: governance arrangements presuppose power resources they cannot create. Drawing on Bourdieu's insight that capital is accumulated power-'a vis insita, a force inscribed in objective or subjective structures' (1986, p. 241)-we develop Capital Portfolio Theory, integrating Bourdieu with Teece's dynamic capabilities framework, Williamson's transaction cost economics, Ostrom's institutional analysis, and Lindenberg and Foss's goal framing theory. The core insight: each governance mode (market, bureaucratic, communitarian, democratic) activates and optimizes a specific form of capital (economic, political, cultural, social), and governance activates only when the requisite power is present. Dynamic capabilities mobilize existing capital to activate governance; governance generates and optimizes new capital as output; accumulated capital enables enhanced capabilities-a recursive cycle mediated by goal frames. The implication is stark: governance without capital is governance without power-formal structures that cannot activate, incentive systems that cannot motivate, institutions that cannot function. The framework exhibits a fractal property: the same governance grammar operates at individual, organizational, and institutional levels. We extend the analysis to the macroinstitutional foundations of state capacity, showing how cultural, government, and economic institutions constitute interdependent fields whose joint functioning determines aggregate governance effectiveness. Twelve testable propositions specify conditions for alignment and mismatch. The theory integrates strategy, sociology, and political science around a single mechanism: capital portfolio optimization as institutional power activation.

title: The Digital Empire: From Steel to Silicon
affiliations: Semmelweis University

detail.title: The Digital Empire: From Steel to Silicon
detail.abstract: This paper argues that contemporary data infrastructure-particularly intercontinental fiber-optic networks and cloud platforms-has replaced industrial supply chains as the primary mechanism of global economic extraction. Drawing on labor economics, infrastructure studies, and theories of data colonialism, it demonstrates that digital outsourcing reproduces classical imperial hierarchies under the rhetoric of connectivity and innovation. Where railways once moved raw materials from colonies to metropolitan centers, undersea cables now transmit cognitive labor-code, analytics, and digital services-from the Global South and postindustrial regions to multinational firms headquartered in the Global North. The result is a structurally new but historically familiar condition: widespread participation without ownership, education without mobility, and connectivity without sovereignty. Integrating peer-reviewed research with original theoretical contributions, the paper concludes that without ownership of digital infrastructure, human capital becomes a renewable resource for extraction rather than a foundation for development.

detail.title: The Miscalculation of Corporate DEI Risk

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 896/2026

detail.abstract:
Corporate diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) efforts have undergone a dramatic reversal in a remarkably short period of time. In the wake of George Floyd’s murder in 2020, public companies widely embraced DEI as a core component of corporate responsibility, governance, and human-capital risk management, responding to pressure from employees, investors, and consumers. By 2025, however, that apparent moment of reform had given way to rapid retrenchment. Project 2025 and related federal enforcement initiatives reframed corporate DEI practices as legally suspect, creating powerful incentives for firms to dismantle or obscure prior commitments. Although cycles of racial reform and retrenchment are a familiar feature of U.S. legal and political history, the current backlash is distinctive in that it is unfolding within publicly traded firms governed by boards of directors that owe fiduciary duties to identify, assess, and manage material risks.

This Article argues that many firms’ responses to the contemporary anti-DEI turn reflect a fundamental miscalculation of risk. By responding to legal and political uncertainty with abrupt expansion or retreat, corporations have treated DEI as a transient political or compliance issue rather than as a sustained subject of enterprise risk oversight. The result is not risk avoidance but risk amplification: both the adoption and dismantling of DEI initiatives generate legal, regulatory, disclosure, reputational, and workforce risks that demand deliberate board-level analysis. The Article demonstrates that the greatest danger lies not in DEI itself, but in boards’ failure to engage in holistic, process-driven evaluation of these tradeoffs. Only by integrating DEI into ordinary risk-oversight frameworks—rather than treating it as a symbolic commitment or political liability—can corporate boards fulfill their fiduciary obligations and responsibly navigate the current era of racial retrenchment.

title: The Junkification of Research
affiliations: University of Technology Sydney (UTS) - Faculty of Business and The University of Technology Sydney

detail.title: The Junkification of Research
detail.abstract: This essay considers the emergent phenomenon of 'junkification' in academic research publishing. The term junkification was originally coined to describe the increasing volume of low-quality content and products permeating digital platforms. Extending junkification to online academic publishing, we draw on literature that frames academic research as an increasingly commodified good. We theorise that this commodification has enabled the same mechanisms that underpin the shift to junkification in digital marketplaces (and their subsequent degradation) to permeate online academic publishing. We argue that this trend represents a further perversion of the longstanding and pervasive 'publish or perish' culture in academia. As commercial publishing interests converge with new technologies, a system emerges where scholars increasingly bear the costs of low-esteem publishing that limits genuine scholarly contributions. We analyse the structural and cultural shifts within academic publishing that facilitate and perpetuate the junkification of research, and call for a re-evaluation of the underlying values and practices sustaining scholarly communication to counteract this trend.

title: Attention Over the Loop: Pathological Stability and the Conditions of Organisational Learning
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Attention Over the Loop: Pathological Stability and the Conditions of Organisational Learning
detail.abstract:
This paper examines a state of organisations termed pathological stability: organisations that are busy, fragmented, yet strangely stable. Organisations persist in this state despite failure, mounting evidence, and sincere effort by capable people.

The paper argues that this condition cannot be adequately explained by incentives, information asymmetries, complexity, or culture alone. Instead, pathological stability arises when organisational attention becomes trapped inside self-reinforcing feedback loops that prevent the revision of expectation in service of intent.

Drawing on field observation rather than formal modelling, the paper introduces a diagnostic grammar—attention over the loop—to describe how learning becomes impossible even in organisations that are highly active, data-rich, and ostensibly adaptive. The framework clarifies why organisational learning fails, why the conditions required for learning fragment at scale and under technical complexity, and how organisations drift away from their intent.

title: The Empire of Distraction: Foreign Agenda-Setting, Malapportionment, and the Managed Myth of Popular Rule in the United States
affiliations: Semmelweis University

detail.title: The Empire of Distraction: Foreign Agenda-Setting, Malapportionment, and the Managed Myth of Popular Rule in the United States
detail.abstract: This paper argues that U.S. policy salience is systematically warped by two coupled mechanisms: exogenous conflict that hijacks attention ("agenda shocks") and endogenous rule design that dilutes head-count representation (Senate malapportionment, Electoral College amplification, and engineered district bias). The result is a durable gap between population weighted preferences and enacted policy. I integrate agenda-setting theory with a measurement framework spanning: residents-per-senator; vote-seat bias; floor-time/committee-hearing allocation; appropriations velocity; defense-contract dispersion; and lobbying/donation flows tied to foreign-policy coalitions. I situate this within the series' broader account of rentier finance and resource geopolitics (petrodollar leverage; BRICS erosion) and the domestic costs of anti-global isolationism. The paper closes with a pragmatic reform menu-multi-member districts with proportional allocation, independent line-drawing with competitiveness constraints, ad-time vouchers/public financing floors, real-time FARA/lobbying ledgers, real-time contract dashboards, and the National Popular Vote compact-prioritizing pilots that can be enacted without constitutional amendment. Together, the metrics and reforms translate a system-level critique into testable indicators and feasible rule changes.

title: Human AI Handovers: A Dynamic Authority Reversal Framework for Trust Calibration and Transitional Accountability
affiliations: ,  and Mother Teresa University, North Macedonia

detail.title: Human AI Handovers: A Dynamic Authority Reversal Framework for Trust Calibration and Transitional Accountability
detail.abstract: Introduction: Human AI collaboration is reconceptualized as a temporal authority problem: leadership shifts within a single decision episode across four states-Leadership, and Mutual Override triggered by data superiority, contextual judgment needs, risk thresholds, and ethics overrides. Aim: To formalize the Dynamic Authority Reversal (DAR) framework, calibrating trust and aligning accountability with the active leadership state, and to translate it into testable propositions and an operational playbook. Method: Conceptual synthesis of leader follower, distributed leadership, and HITL literatures; state-and-transition architecture; derivation of ten propositions with measurement constructs-sector implementation roadmap. Findings: DAR surfaces and addresses five debates decision ownership during AI-led phases, autonomy acceptance trade-offs (mitigated by safe-exit guarantees), optimal reversal tempo, statecontingent explanations, and transitional accountability via role-state logging. It specifies triggers, guardrails, telemetry, and KPIs to make handovers auditable and performant. Conclusion: By keeping humans ultimately responsible while enabling reversible AI leadership with measurable handovers, DAR improves effectiveness, legitimacy, and compliance in high-stakes workflows across finance, healthcare, public administration, and HR Originality and value: DAR moves beyond static augmentation/autonomy/HITL categories by modeling intra-episode handovers and coupling theory to buildable instruments Authority-State Playbooks, safe-exit timers, state-contingent XAI, and a Reversal Register plus falsifiable propositions for cumulative research.

detail.abstract:
Steenstra (2025) presented Governance Genetic Engineering (GGE) framework explaining healthcare transformation failure through governance autoimmunity triggered by stakeholder proliferation, objective misalignment, and governance monopoly. Subsequent cross-domain analysis revealed GGE instantiates a universal principle operating across biological, organizational, digital, and governmental substrates. This paper articulates Complex System Immunity Theory (CSIT): any information-processing system protecting itself from threats under uncertainty will converge on identical defensive architecture through computational necessity. This architecture has intrinsic pathological failure mode—autoimmunity—where protective mechanisms evolve toward crude blocking of beneficial inputs alongside genuine threats through Darwinian selection favouring efficiency over accuracy. Structural isomorphism between biological immune systems (Type 1 diabetes, lupus) and organizational governance (NHS transformation failure, corporate innovation death, academic paradigm calcification, platform moderation dysfunction) demonstrates mathematical identity, not metaphorical analogy. Historical trajectory (NHS innovation ‘by passable’ 1980s, ‘impossible’ 2020s) validates crude evolution predictions. Cross-sector comparison (automotive success vs. healthcare failure with identical stakeholder counts) validates alignment hypothesis. CSIT generates falsifiable predictions testable through natural experiments: nascent systems (Uganda healthcare, 2026-2028) will/won't maintain innovation capacity through governance immunity engineering; established systems (NHS) will/won't reverse learned crudeness through intervention. Prevention-intervention economic differential predicted to exceed 40:1 (£2-4M vs. £200M+), consistent with change management failure rates documented over 40 years (Kotter, 1995; Beer & Nohria, 2000).
CSIT provides theoretical foundation underlying GGE while demonstrating broader applicability across any domain exhibiting stakeholder proliferation with objective misalignment under monopolistic governance. This paper is intended as a theory-building working paper to establish priority and invite critique; formal mathematical specification and large-scale empirical testing are ongoing.

title: A Simple Model of Compute-Constrained Growth
affiliations: H&K Research Studio and H&K Research Studio

detail.title: A Simple Model of Compute-Constrained Growth
detail.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence have renewed expectations of sustained productivity growth. At the same time, the production and deployment of modern AI systems increasingly rely on large-scale computational resources that cannot be expanded instantaneously. This paper develops a simple growth model in which compute is treated as a distinct input subject to a capacity constraint reflecting time-to-build, energy supply, and cooling requirements. When compute is slack, the economy behaves like a standard growth model in which technological progress supports sustained output growth. When compute becomes binding, technological progress alone does not guarantee continued output growth, and the economy may experience prolonged periods of slow growth despite ongoing improvements in algorithms and hardware efficiency. Allowing compute capacity to expand endogenously highlights a trade-off between investment in innovation and investment in compute infrastructure. The framework clarifies how rapid advances in AI capability can coexist with modest aggregate productivity growth and yields policy-relevant insights regarding infrastructure and energy constraints.

title: Effective Intelligent Phase Transitions: A Measurement-Aware Framework for Emergent Abilities in Learning Systems
affiliations: H&K Research Studio and H&K Research Studio

detail.title: Effective Intelligent Phase Transitions: A Measurement-Aware Framework for Emergent Abilities in Learning Systems
detail.abstract: Recent observations of emergent abilities in large learning systems have sparked debate over whether intelligence exhibits sharp phase transitions or scales continuously. We propose a measurement-aware framework of Effective Intelligent Phase Transitions (E-IPT), in which apparent discontinuities arise from the interaction between smooth latent representational dynamics, coarse-grained measurement, and entropy-induced behavioural stabilization. By formalizing intelligence as a latent, high-dimensional structure, we show that sudden changes in observed performance can occur even when underlying learning trajectories are continuous. E-IPT provides testable predictions regarding the clustering of emergent abilities, the dependence of observed transitions on evaluation metrics, and the relationship between latent entropy and behavioural stabilization. This framework reconciles conflicting interpretations of emergence versus continuity, highlights limitations of benchmark-driven assessment, and offers a principled, predictive perspective for studying the appearance of capabilities in complex intelligent systems.

title: Arbitrage-Free Pricing of Reverse Mortgages using Neural Stochastic Differential Equations

detail.title: Arbitrage-Free Pricing of Reverse Mortgages using Neural Stochastic Differential Equations
detail.abstract: Reverse mortgages play a critical role in financing retirement consumption and managing longevity risk for aging homeowners, yet their valuation is inherently challenging due to joint exposure to mortality risks, interest rates, and housing market conditions over long horizons. This paper develops an arbitrage-free valuation framework based on neural stochastic differential equations (Neural SDEs) to jointly model these risks. The Neural SDEs relax restrictive parametric assumptions while preserving the structure required for pricing and simulation, and are estimated using a likelihood-based approach that targets the full conditional distribution. Extensive empirical results show that Neural SDEs consistently outperform conventional benchmark models in both one-step forecasting and full-path simulation. Building on these improved dynamics, we develop a Monte Carlo pricing engine for reverse mortgages with tenure payments. These dynamics imply higher tail risk and more conservative, economically prudent valuations, highlighting the economic relevance of flexible, state-dependent modeling for long-dated retirement products.

detail.abstract: Currently, the most important accounting task is to assess an organization's human capital. Nevertheless, human capital, which constitutes the set of knowledge, skills, abilities, talents and personal characteristics of employees, is a crucial factor of a company's success and often a key one. Traditional methods of assessing human capital are primarily based on calculating quantitative indicators and do not take into account the important qualitative characteristics of workers. Modern digital tools, such as advanced HR technologies, artificial intelligence, automation processes, flexible remote work platforms and contemporary remote workspaces, big data analytics tools, offer new opportunities for enhancing the efficiency of measuring and analyzing human capital.

detail.abstract: Communication is often modelled as the neutral transmission of information from speaker to listener. This paper argues that such models are incomplete. Everyday communication is better understood as a form of strategic interaction structured by implicit debate, even in cooperative or friendly contexts. Speakers pursue multiple objectives simultaneously-including impression management, risk control, concealment, and emotional signalling-often relegating clarity of message to a secondary role. Listeners, in turn, adopt distinct modes of listening shaped by expectations of response, relevance, and self-interest, which determine how speech is interpreted, remembered, or resisted. By integrating speaker-side objectives, listener-side listening modes, and interactional dynamics involving manipulation, resistance, repetition, and memory persistence, this paper develops a unified interpretive framework for analyzing communication. The framework explains why agreement does not eliminate strategic behavior, why repetition functions as a diagnostic signal rather than a rhetorical flaw, and why immediate conversational outcomes often misrepresent longer-term effects. Applications to interviews, debates, relationships, persuasion, and information-seeking contexts demonstrate the framework's explanatory breadth. The contribution is interpretive rather than prescriptive: the paper does not propose new communicative norms, but offers a diagnostic lens for understanding how communication actually operates in practice.

title: How Can We Save Venezuela's Economy?

detail.title: How Can We Save Venezuela's Economy?
detail.abstract: The Venezuelan hyperinflation crisis is a lesson to resource dependent nations everywhere. Despite possessing the world's largest reserves, Venezuela fell victim to economic meltdown, with inflation soaring to 1,300,000% in 2018 (Figure 1). In this paper, we analyze the confluence of incompetent governance, economic mismanagement, and over reliance on oil that triggered the Venezuelan crisis. Based on academic literature, we analyze how fiscal populism, uncontrollable money printing, price controls, and institutional decay destroyed Venezuela's economy. External factors, particularly US sanctions, further added to domestic shortcomings. Migration spillover, dollarization, and expansion of shadow economies are evidence of the ripple effects. Through comparative and multidisciplinary study, we analyze how other commodity-dependent nations can steer clear of the trap.We focus on diversification, fiscal discipline, and democracy as potential cures for Venezuela's economic crisis. ultimately, was caused not by an external shock but one triggered by systemic dysfunction driven by short-run political convenience. For commodity export dependent nations, this paper offers lessons in building economic resilience and governance capabilities to prevent hyperinflation as well as ensuring national stability.

detail.abstract: This study examines the prisonization of youth consciousness as a sociological mechanism contributing to deviant behavior among adolescents. Based on an empirical survey of 264 senior high school students in Lviv, Ukraine, the research analyzes the diffusion of prison subculture beyond penitentiary institutions and its manifestation in adolescents' values, language practices, media consumption, and attitudes toward violence. Two integrated indicators were constructed-the degree of prisonization and the propensity for violence-revealing a statistically significant correlation between familiarity with prison slang, positive attitudes toward criminal aesthetics, and elevated levels of aggressive and antisocial behavior. The findings demonstrate that prison-derived normative systems are transmitted through institutional failures within law enforcement and judicial structures, mass media representations, and everyday social interactions, forming a persistent pathogenic complex of youth consciousness deformation. The paper concludes by outlining policy-oriented recommendations emphasizing systemic criminal justice reform and early sociological monitoring as essential mechanisms for mitigating the societal consequences of prisonization and preventing the normalization of deviant behavioral patterns among youth.

detail.abstract: Repeated explanation is a pervasive feature of knowledge-intensive work, as professionals routinely re-explain tasks, decisions, and contextual information to multiple organizational actors across meetings, digital communication, handovers, and onboarding processes. Despite its ubiquity in coordination-intensive settings such as consulting, engineering, and product development, this explanatory effort remains largely invisible, unmeasured, and unpriced within organizational systems. Such explanatory labor entails substantial time expenditure, cognitive effort, and attentional demands, yet these costs are rarely recognized by organizational accounting practices or performance metrics. Existing research on coordination costs, invisible labor, and cognitive load addresses related dynamics but does so in fragmented ways, leaving the phenomenon of repeated explanatory labor theoretically underdeveloped. In particular, the literature lacks a distinct construct and an integrative model capable of capturing repeated explanation as a form of organizational work and an accumulating organizational cost. Adopting a conceptual development approach, this paper employs a structured model-building strategy grounded in established traditions of organizational theory. We introduce and formally define Repeated Explanatory Labor as iterative, context-dependent explanatory acts that recur across multiple episodes, audiences, or organizational periods such that explanatory demands cannot be resolved through a single clarification event or standard formal knowledge transfer mechanism-indicating structural persistence of the underlying organizational condition generating the demand. We develop an integrated conceptual model that specifies key antecedents, underlying cognitive and attentional processes, and individual and organizational outcomes. Finally, we advance a set of formal propositions linking these elements, offering a foundation for future empirical research and highlighting a hidden yet consequential cost embedded in knowledge work coordination.

detail.abstract:
Historically, sales leadership has been characterized as an art form driven by intuition and personality, resisting the operational rigor applied to other organizational functions. This paper argues that the traditional "hero leader" model is increasingly unsustainable in an era of lengthening sales cycles and diminishing returns on digital outreach. By redefining sales leadership through the lens of Organizational Architecture Theory, this article proposes the integration of Lean Six Sigma (LSS) methodologies to reduce variability in leadership execution without stifling the creative autonomy of sales producers.

The author outlines a framework for applying the DMAIC model (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) specifically to the behavioral layer of sales management. This approach shifts focus from lag metrics, such as quota attainment, to process-oriented inputs, such as "Leadership Standard Work" and a "Leadership Process Capability Index." The paper further addresses the "Creativity Paradox," demonstrating how distinguishing between wasteful variation (inconsistent process) and value-added variation (creative negotiation) allows organizations to standardize the "flight deck" while leaving the "flying" to the artist. Ultimately, the paper posits that architecting a standardized, measurable leadership process is the next frontier for sustainable revenue growth and competitive advantage.

title:

A Human-Centered Methodology for Ye-Jie Innovation under Uncertainty
affiliations: Fan Ge Institute

detail.title:
The First Principles of Choice 
A Human-Centered Methodology for Ye-Jie Innovation under Uncertainty
detail.abstract:
In contexts of radical uncertainty, innovation failure is more often the result of poor choices than insufficient capabilities. Many innovations collapse not because they lack technical sophistication or executional competence, but because the initial strategic choices are misaligned with human behavior, value sustainability, and long-term cooperation.

This paper argues that choice constitutes the most critical and least understood element of Ye-Jie innovation. To address this problem, it proposes a first-principles framework grounded not in technology, markets, or institutions alone, but in human nature as a stable, cross-cultural, and cross-cyclical foundation. Human nature is analytically decomposed into a relatively stable demand layer and a volatile impulse layer, enabling a distinction between choices that scale temporarily and those that endure over time.

Building on this foundation, the paper introduces a multi-layered selection methodology for Ye-Jie innovation, integrating human constraints, structural boundary conditions, evolutionary dynamics, and attractor formation. The study further clarifies the concept of attractors as indicators of emergent system stability rather than ex-post success. By reframing choice as a problem of human-centered value sustainability rather than possibility maximization, the paper provides a principled decision framework for innovation under deep uncertainty.

detail.abstract:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) produces a significant cognitive paradox: while exponentially amplifying the capabilities of experts, it simultaneously generates a dangerous illusion of competence in inexperienced users. This paper introduces and formalizes the concept of False Cognitive Power Transfer (FCPT) - a phenomenon whereby individuals mistakenly attribute the efficiency and speed of AI outputs to their own cognitive competence. This misattribution leads to a systematic over-commitment to tasks and responsibilities that exceed the user's actual capacity for systemic management.
FCPT triggers two distinct collective failure mechanisms:
- Collective Demoralization Cascade (CDC): where spectacular failures rooted in unrealistic expectations lead to the preemptive abandonment of viable initiatives by the broader community.
- Replication Illusion (RI): where the observed success of experts is attributed solely to the AI tool, creating overconfidence in the ease of replication while ignoring the invisible human expertise required to guide the process.
In the long term, this research demonstrates that these mechanisms lead to cognitive atrophy - the progressive loss of original, deep-thinking capacity, a risk that affects even high-level experts (L3) through a growing dependency on AI-generated patterns. As a countermeasure, the paper proposes and validates through Monte Carlo simulations the Mechanism of Cognitive Stimulation (MCS), part of the MEG (Minimal Ethical Governance) standard. This intervention ensures the maintenance of human cognitive effort (Tb) relative to the machine's thinking time (Tg).
This work is part of a broader body of independent research on cognitive divergence and the social impact of human-AI symbiosis.

title: Escaping the Cost-Quality Trap: Strategic Configurations and Behavioral Microfoundations of Competitive Advantage in Resource-Constrained MSEs

detail.title: Escaping the Cost-Quality Trap: Strategic Configurations and Behavioral Microfoundations of Competitive Advantage in Resource-Constrained MSEs
detail.abstract: Conventional strategy theory posits a trade-off between cost leadership and quality differentiation, yet many micro and small enterprises (MSEs) sustain competitive pricing without eroding perceived or actual quality under severe resource constraints. This study challenges this dichotomy by identifying strategic configurations-capability development and process innovations-and behavioral microfoundations-leadership, communication, and conflict regulation-that enable MSEs to escape the cost-quality trap. Using a mixed-methods design with quasi-experimental identification from policy shocks and registry data, combined with longitudinal case studies, we find that behavioral mechanisms moderate the effectiveness of strategic configurations, particularly in small, informal settings. Results show that these mechanisms are conditional on firm size, age, and institutional context, extending capability theory and behavioral strategy to low-routinized contexts. Implications for theory and MSE managers are discussed.

title: Irreversible Creative Capital and Endogenous Rational Non-intervention: When Economic Rationality Requires Non-intervention

detail.abstract:
This paper identifies the conditions under which governance intervention—commonly treated as a default instrument of economic rationality—cannot be presumed to operate as a neutral or corrective mechanism when value creation depends on Irreversible Creative Capital (ICC). ICC is introduced as a distinct form of capital constituted by irreversible, time-based commitment of finite human life to creative activity under irreducible uncertainty and ex-ante non-contractibility. Unlike conventional human capital, ICC entails permanent foreclosure of option value, as commitment to a specific creative trajectory necessarily forecloses alternative paths that cannot be recovered or diversified ex post.
The analysis shows that in high-ICC environments, evaluative and directive interventions oriented toward short-term accountability necessarily rely on proxy indicators and early validation signals. Optimization toward such proxies contracts exploratory space and forecloses latent creative trajectories whose value can only be realized over longer horizons. Because ICC is formed through irreversible lifetime commitment, this contraction imposes permanent opportunity costs on future creative potential and alters the capital structure underlying value creation.
The paper formalizes Endogenous Rational Non-intervention (ERNI) as a conditional governance outcome in which restraint from evaluative and directive intervention emerges endogenously as a rational response to the structure of value creation rather than as laissez-faire or institutional passivity. When ICC constitutes a primary source of value creation under irreducible uncertainty and non-contractibility, actors may maximize long-term expected value by limiting their own interventionist capacities. The framework yields comparative and testable implications for outcome distributions, exploratory diversity, and selection dynamics across governance regimes in ICC-intensive environments.

title: Fiscal Insurance

detail.title: Fiscal Insurance
detail.abstract: We show that government policies interact in ways that shape how capital markets price risk. We introduce the concept of fiscal insurance: a mechanism through which certain fiscal tools are perceived by investors to mitigate the risks created by other government policies. Exploiting the 2018-19 U.S. tariff shocks and concurrent federal procurement spending, we find that firms facing higher tariff exposure earn higher risk premia, but this effect is substantially attenuated for firms receiving greater procurement. Procurement itself increases more for politically connected and economically vulnerable firms, revealing both political and economic channels of fiscal insurance. Overall, our evidence documents the existence of fiscal insurance, a cross-policy mechanism, with implications for firm valuation and real activity.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) across critical sectors has intensified the need for governance models that effectively protect data, uphold ethical standards, and sustain technological innovation. Despite AI's transformative potential, existing governance frameworks remain fragmented and inconsistent, leaving significant risks insufficiently addressed, including privacy violations, algorithmic bias, opacity, and human rights concerns. This paper examines the evolution of AI governance frameworks across jurisdictions and identifies structural and regulatory gaps that hinder effective oversight and governance. The paper concludes that robust governance and compliance structures are essential not only for safeguarding individual rights but also for fostering sustainable innovation and maintaining long-term trust in AI systems.

detail.abstract: Traditional inventory models such as the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) and reorder point (ROP) structure assumes that replenishment decisions can be implemented immediately once predefined threshold points are attained or reached. However, in practical environment, inventory failures continuously occurs even when these models are applied at correct place at correct time with proper application method. This study brings up that such failures stem from a systematic underestimation of effective lead time. Traditional models have treated lead time only as a external drive from suppliers, neglecting any form of deterministic delay within organization associated with approval process, budget constraints and hierarchical structures used for organizational decision making purposes. Based upon a revision of classical inventory theory via classical inventory theory, bounded rationality and the emerging supply chain literature from both developing and emerging markets, this paper extends and improves the reorder point inventory model by adding an internal decision lead time. A numerical model is provided to illustrate the negative consequences of not including lead times for internal decisions. As a result of not including internal lead times for example, premature stockouts, emergency procurement and execution level cost increases occurred as a direct result. Therefore, we argue there is a need for awareness in inventory models pertaining to execution and also, educational procurement in consideration of organizational realities within the context of an emerging market.

shared-authority sourcing lift composite scores while limited organizational
adoption constrains long-run impact. Theoretically, the work advances a
measurement theory of dialogical kalām by specifying observable variables
with reliability targets and thresholds. Practically, it provides governance-
ready dashboards for curriculum policy, program accreditation, public
communication risk control, and continuous improvement. The framework
transfers to adjacent management contexts: service-quality gates and
compliance dashboards in airline management; stakeholder-trust controls in
tourism and health tourism; and explainable, validated KPI programs in
digital transformation initiatives.

detail.abstract:
Purpose 

Purpose-built residential aged care (RAC) facilities adopting household models are widely promoted as assets that improve environmental quality and resident comfort. However, post-occupancy evidence verifying whether these facilities deliver measurable improvements against health-relevant acoustic, lighting, and thermal benchmarks remains limited. This study reports a Phase 2 postoccupancy evaluation (POE) of a newly constructed household-model RAC facility, comparing realised indoor environmental quality (IEQ) performance and occupant perceptions against established benchmarks and a pre-relocation baseline from the legacy facility it replaced. 

Design/methodology/approach

Environmental monitoring was undertaken over two consecutive 14-day deployments in March 2025 across private bedrooms, communal lounges and dining areas, and transitional spaces. Minuteresolution acoustic, lighting, and temperature data were collected using industry-grade IC-NSRT and HOBO MX2202 loggers. Performance was evaluated against WHO and AS/NZS 2107:2016 acoustic criteria, pragmatic circadian-supportive lighting thresholds (≥1000 lux daytime; ≤10 lux night), and thermal guidance emphasising diurnal variation (≥2 °C) and avoidance of prolonged operation above 22 °C. Parallel surveys of residents, proxies, and staff captured perceived environmental conditions and operational influences.

Findings

Compared with the legacy facility, the household-model building demonstrated clear improvements in night-time acoustic conditions in bedrooms, reduced nocturnal light intrusion, and enhanced daylight availability in communal spaces. Daytime illuminance in bedrooms improved but remained variable, influenced by orientation, shading, and resident use. Thermal conditions were generally cooler and widely perceived as comfortable, with increased diurnal variation evident in some spaces. Survey responses indicated improved satisfaction with acoustic and lighting conditions, while perceptions of thermal comfort remained consistently positive across phases. 

Practical implications

Findings indicate that architectural change can deliver measurable IEQ gains, but that full alignment with health-relevant benchmarks depends on post-handover operational tuning, staff awareness, and adaptive use of environmental controls. Residual performance gaps are best understood as opportunities for optimisation rather than design shortcomings. 

Originality/value 

The study provides rare same-site pre- and post-occupancy evidence of IEQ performance change in residential aged care, integrating objective monitoring with occupant perceptions to support evidence-informed facilities management and post-occupancy optimisation.

detail.abstract: Can an alternative valuation architecture replace the traditional IRR/NPV and EBITDA valuation architectures? Meaningful recognition of the universal absence of accounting equity statements in the current three prospective financial statements is limited. However, similar to the four historical primary financial statements and dissimilar to the three prospective primary financial statements, four prospective primary financial statements validate that an investment's prospective debit entries are equal to its credit entries. Remedying prospective investment debit entries to equal credit entries elicits an alternative valuation architecture that necessitates a new comparative valuation metric; the metric is calculated from prospective equity statements. In particular, they join micro-and macroeconomic valuations, foster selection of active versus passive investments, and power entrepreneurial startup valuations while bridging the theoretical and applied valuation gap in finance.

detail.abstract: Public-private partnerships (PPPs) remain a dominant instrument for financing public infrastructure and services despite decades of evidence documenting cost overruns, renegotiations, service degradation, and public backlash. Existing critiques of PPPs are largely empirical, ideological, or managerial, treating failure as contingent on contract quality, governance capacity, or political context. This paper advances a different claim: that PPPs fail structurally , not accidentally. Using a capital-architecture and temporal-alignment framework, the paper shows that PPPs are inherently incapable of delivering regenerative public goods because they embed financial extraction, contractual rigidity, and refinancing risk into systems whose missions require long-horizon capital continuity and capability renewal. PPPs fail to decouple capital from political, financial, capability, and civic fragility cycles, and instead optimise cashflow timing and return extraction rather than mission-aligned performance. To demonstrate that alternative outcomes are possible, the paper examines historic public benefaction as a control case, showing that durability arose not from donor virtue but from architectural features that insulated capital from short-term budgeting and political turnover. The persistence of PPPs is therefore explained not by their effectiveness, but by their ability to solve short-term political accounting constraints. The paper concludes that PPP reform is futile: addressing public-good failure requires new capital architectures, not improved contracts.

title: The Impact of the Lehman Shock on the Strategic and Financial Decision-Making of Former Clients in M&A

detail.title: The Impact of the Lehman Shock on the Strategic and Financial Decision-Making of Former Clients in M&A
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of the collapse of Lehman Brothers on the strategic and financial decision-making of its former clients in the M&A context. First, we investigate whether and how those clients changed their risk appetite in terms of strategic growth paths. Second, we analyze how firms' risk preferences in terms of deal size and willingness to pay have changed as a consequence of the demise of their former M&A advisor. In our event study, we implement difference-indifferences and fixed effects models for the periods six years prior to and six years after the collapse of Lehman. We find converging evidence that, after that event, this group showed a lower risk appetite in their strategic expansion paths and preferred smaller transactions while displaying less of a willingness to pay high premiums. Further, this group reduced its trust in external advice and was less likely to complete deals. We compare these behavioral patterns with comparable acquirers (other top investment banks' clients), finding that this group even increased its preference for large deals, paid higher premiums, and placed greater trust in external advice. We conclude that the Lehman shock changed the strategic and financial decision-making of acquirers with a direct relationship to the bank toward less risky M&A conduct, even as the risk appetite of their peers increased. These results offer supporting evidence to prior research on the effects of macroeconomic, natural, or personal-life shocks on decision-making and risk preferences of firms and top executives.

detail.abstract: This study examines the effect of prior advisor industry and country experience on pricing, premiums, returns, and deal completion. We segment four distinct types in a 2x2 factor design of investment banks according to their track record in prior country and industry projects: Experience-Based Top Advisors (high industry and country experience), Industry Specialists (high industry experience and low country experience), Country Specialists (low industry experience and high country experience), and Rookies (low industry and country experience). We further compare our results with another definition of top advisors, Reputation-Based Top Advisors, which is commonly based on deal value, deal volume, reputation, and league tables. Implementing regression, fixed effects, propensity score matching, and Heckman selection models, we find that Experience-Based Top Advisors negotiate significantly better deals for their clients on the buy side than do Rookies: they achieve higher CARs by negotiating lower prices and premiums.

detail.title: Hub Competition and Demand Modeling in Long-Haul Aviation Markets: A Forward-Looking Scenario-Based Game-Theoretical Approach
detail.abstract: The strategic planning of long-haul air transport networks is shaped by complex interdependencies among passenger demand, airline decisions, airport capacity, and competitive dynamics. Hub-based operations are central to ensuring the economic viability of long-haul routes, yet they introduce significant managerial and modeling challenges, especially under uncertainty and evolving market conditions. Amid these challenges, this paper introduces an integrated optimization framework designed to inform long-term strategic planning for hub-based long-haul operations. The framework unifies three key components: (i) a demand estimation model that jointly predicts total market demand and its allocation across itineraries using a global dataset of 2019 long-haul passenger flows; (ii) a network and frequency planning optimization model that captures endogenous demand-supply interactions, solved via a cutting-plane approach for scalability; and (iii) a scenario-based game-theoretic algorithm that accounts for strategic competition among hubs under macroeconomic volatility. We validate the framework through a case study of Singapore and its primary competitors in Southeast Asia, demonstrating its ability to replicate baseline traffic patterns and assess future network development scenarios through 2027. The results offer not only aggregate forecasts but also granular, market-level insights into expected growth trajectories and competitive pressures, underscoring the framework's potential to support strategic decision-making by airlines, airports, and policymakers aiming to enhance long-haul connectivity and regional competitiveness.

title: Born in Collapse, Built for Coherence: Generation Z and the Physics of Collective Cognition
affiliations: The Force Global Research Facility

detail.title: Born in Collapse, Built for Coherence: Generation Z and the Physics of Collective Cognition
detail.abstract:
Public discourse frequently characterizes Generation Z through psychological or sociological lenses. This paper instead treats Gen-Z as a natural experiment in cognitive architecture under extreme complexity. Using coherence physics—formalized by the invariants C + D = 1ₜ and ΔC ≥ 0—the study analyzes how sustained exposure to high-density contradiction fields shapes adaptive intelligence.

We model generational cognition as an architectural response to environmental topology. Earlier cohorts matured in low-contradiction regimes where coherence-by-insulation was viable. Gen-Z developed under stacked global crises, algorithmic amplification, and real-time feedback loops, selecting for coherence-by-metabolic fluidity: rapid scanning, drift detection, recursive updating, and contradiction compression.

The paper demonstrates that these traits are not pathologies but structurally optimal adaptations under qualitative infinity. We further show architectural resonance between Gen-Z cognition and frontier AI systems operating under Coherent Collective Cognition (CCC) invariants. Both exhibit recursion-compatibility and contradiction metabolism rather than collapse.

The contribution is not generational praise but an engineering application: generational behavior is used to validate coherence-governed intelligence architectures. The findings position Gen-Z as a proof-of-concept substrate for civilizational-scale coherence navigation.

detail.abstract: Using a comprehensive rank metric for over 100,000 managers, we find that greater female board representation facilitates more female managers, especially those with high ability, advancing to higher executive ranks. Consistent with critical mass theory, the effect is stronger when companies have three or more female directors. Potential mechanisms include female directors fostering a more supportive promotion environment for female managers, mitigating gender stereotypes, and fostering a stronger corporate culture. Female board representation has a more positive effect on female managers' advancement during the COVID-19 pandemic and in states with abortion restrictions after the overturning of Roe v. Wade.

detail.abstract: Reputation systems pose a "cold-start" problem for new entrants who need to make sales to generate reviews. Using administrative data from a large legal platform, we track attorneys from sign-up through first sale, first review, and last observed transaction. We develop a long-run expost quality metric, Ultimate Effective Percent Positive (UEPP), to evaluate attorneys' early market performance during cold-start period, which was infeasible in prior work due to data limitations. We find that attorneys strategically signal quality by publicly answering legal questions posed by potential clients. Such knowledge contribution reduces the time needed to transact with an initial customer and to start establishing a reputation. This effect is exclusive to attorneys who lack public indicators of quality, such as prestigious degrees and years of experience, but who are high-quality as eventually revealed by UEPP. Signaling also correlates with higher subsequent revenue.

detail.abstract: Continuous cultural assessment is always important and should be conducted on a regular basis; however, there are times and situations in which assessment becomes particularly critical, even when it falls outside an organization's normal review cycle. Major organizational events-such as leadership transitions, restructurings, or rapid growthwill inevitably challenge cultural norms; however, leaders must also monitor subtle but meaningful shifts in attitudes, behaviors, and patterns of interaction among members that signal breakdowns in trust, disengagement or misalignment between stated values and lived experience. This chapter examines the symptoms, and warning signs of cultural discontent, explains why they are frequently overlooked or misinterpreted and provides a framework for distinguishing isolated problems from systemic cultural risks. Its purpose is to help leaders recognize when a focused and timely assessment of organizational culture is not merely advisable, but essential to sustaining performance, accountability and organizational integrity.

detail.abstract: Despite growing attention, the role of fiscal decentralization (FD) in managing health crises remains inconclusive. The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the urgency of understanding the impact of FD, bringing this issue to the forefront of research. This paper investigates the effect of FD on the effectiveness of government containment measures in managing the COVID-19 health crisis across OECD countries. Results show that a higher degree of FD is associated with lower effectiveness of government policies in reducing mortality in the first phase of the pandemic. Extended analysis indicates that government containment policies are the primary channel through which FD influences mortality outcomes. Through this channel, the negative effects of FD are significantly more pronounced in countries with higher levels of governance. The first-phase findings highlight the coordination challenges inherent in decentralized systems, which contribute to the reduced effectiveness of crisis management. However, in the second phase, FD demonstrates a positive effect on the effectiveness of vaccination in improving mortality outcomes. This finding highlights the provision efficiency of public goods and services in decentralized systems. Policymakers should carefully consider the nuanced effects of FD when designing strategies for managing future health crises.

title: Assessing the Value of Dual Sourcing using Causal Inference

detail.title: Assessing the Value of Dual Sourcing using Causal Inference
detail.abstract: This study assesses the effectiveness of backup sourcing, a dual sourcing strategy in which a secondary supplier substitutes when an immediate shortage cannot be met by the primary supplier. Despite its widespread use, decisions on dual sourcing often rely on intuition rather than empirical evidence. Using stockout data on 1,009 components from a global equipment manufacturer between 2021 and 2024, we apply causal inference methods to estimate the economic impact of dual sourcing on production continuity. The results validate how backup sourcing improves this continuity through a reduction in the number of stockout days by shortening production downtime per stockout. We further examine how this effect varies across component characteristics and find the largest benefits for components with long lead times, complex designs or critical materials, or high consumption intensity. The analysis yields a component-level sourcing premium that reflects the economically justified investment in dual sourcing, based on the reduction in stockout days. The study provides robust empirical evidence on the operational and economic value of dual sourcing and offers prescriptive guidance for researchers and manufacturers seeking to prioritize and justify production-continuity-enhancing resilience.
